notes: ‘Has come in power’ describes the kingdom as having arrived when it is seen. The saying does not identify a single event as its fulfillment.
The question about the Son of Man's suffering stands alongside Elijah's restoration. The text does not explicitly name Elijah's counterpart here.
The compact Greek is punctuated here as Jesus echoing ‘if you can.’ Its wording connects the father's question about ability with the possibility of believing.
The Greek text followed here has ‘prayer,’ without the addition ‘and fasting’ found in another reading.
The millstone is literally one turned by a donkey, emphasizing its size.
These severe bodily images warn against causing people to stumble. Verses 44 and 46 are absent from the Greek text followed here; the numbering gaps are retained.
‘Salted with fire’ and ‘have salt in yourselves’ preserve difficult images. Their meaning is not reduced to a single explanation in the translation.
vocabulary: Transform; here the change witnessed on the mountain, often called the transfiguration.
Believe or trust / unbelief. The father's reply holds these related words together.
Hand over; the passive leaves the agent unstated here.
Cause to stumble or fall; repeated in the warnings that follow.
Gehenna, a name used here for the place of fiery judgment.

notes: The Greek text followed here says ‘they asked’ without naming the questioners. Another reading explicitly names Pharisees.
The Greek text followed here includes ‘and be joined to his wife’; variation around this clause does not make it absent from this edition.
‘Against her’ is retained in the first saying. The next saying explicitly describes a woman divorcing her husband; neither saying is expanded with an exception from another Gospel.
‘Like a child’ is left as a comparison. The saying does not specify a single quality such as innocence or dependence.
The Greek text followed here does not add ‘for those who trust in riches.’ The preceding verse speaks specifically about wealth.
The return list includes mothers but not fathers, and explicitly includes persecutions.
Cup and baptism remain images in Jesus' reply. The passive ‘have been prepared’ does not name who prepared the places.
‘Ransom for many’ retains the compact release image. The saying does not name a recipient of the ransom.
‘Has made you well’ renders a verb that can also mean ‘has saved you.’ Here it accompanies the recovery of sight and following Jesus.
vocabulary: Road or way; the same word links the encounters and journey toward Jerusalem.
Servant / slave; the stronger social term in verse 44 is retained.
Ransom, a price or means of release.
An address meaning ‘my master’ or ‘my teacher.’

notes: The promise to send the colt back is read here as part of the reply the disciples are to give. The clause can also be read as Jesus describing what the person questioning them will do.
The narrator explicitly says it was not the season for figs. That tension is retained rather than explained away.
The Greek construction can describe a customary departure: ‘whenever evening came, they would leave.’
‘This mountain’ is not identified further. Verse 24 says ‘you have received,’ followed by a future promise; the difference in tense is retained.
Verse 26 is absent from the Greek text followed here. The numbering gap is retained.
The Greek text followed here includes the leaders' question, ‘What should we say?’
vocabulary: Colt or young animal; Mark does not add a second animal.
Hosanna, a cry meaning ‘save, please,’ used here in acclamation.
Temple or temple precincts, the wider sacred complex.
An object, vessel, or item of equipment; here rendered collectively as ‘goods.’
Faith or trust; here directed toward God.
Authority; the repeated subject of the challenge and reply.

notes: The Greek calls the person sent a slave, the same social term used in 10:44.
In Mark's telling, the tenants kill the son before throwing him out of the vineyard.
‘Cornerstone’ renders ‘head of the corner,’ an image of a stone given a decisive place in a building.
The repeated question ‘Should we pay it or should we not?’ belongs to verse 14 in the Greek text followed here.
The comparison says people are ‘like angels,’ not that they become angels.
The confession may also be rendered ‘The Lord is our God, the Lord alone.’ The Greek can be construed in more than one way.
The scribe names heart, understanding, and strength. His reply is not expanded to repeat all four terms of verse 30.
‘The Lord’ and ‘my lord’ are distinct referents within the quotation. The text here says ‘beneath your feet,’ not ‘a footstool.’
The widow's gift follows the warning about devouring widows' houses. The translation preserves Jesus' comparison without adding a command to imitate her or a single explanation of the scene.
vocabulary: Beloved; the same description used of the Son in 9:7.
Herodians, people associated with Herod's cause or rule.
Give back, repay, or render what is due.
Lepton / quadrans, names of small coins. Mark states that the widow's two lepta together equal one quadrans.
Life or means of living; here ‘livelihood.’
